summary.one_liner: A workshop-style tutorial repository for writing a Unix shell from scratch, organized into progressive stages with an expect-based test runner.
summary.what_it_does: The README is the course material for a series of workshops on writing a Unix shell, with a focus on interactive rather than scripting use. It is split into five stages (fork/exec/wait, files and pipes, job control and signals, quoting and expansion, interactivity), each with a description, manpage pointers, and tests. A `validate` script runs the tests against a user's shell executable, and can run a whole stage or a single test. The tests target a vanilla Bourne-flavored shell with some ksh influence, and the README says bash and ksh should pass them. The README also collects supplementary links: a shell execution visualizer, books and tutorials on Unix processes, a list of existing shells to examine, and notes on implementing a shell in various languages.
use_cases: learning how Unix processes, fork, exec and wait work
building a toy shell as a learning project
adding pipes and file descriptor redirection to a shell
implementing job control and signal handling (^C, ^\, ^Z)
checking a shell implementation against a test suite
finding reference shells and tutorials to study
how_to_run: Install expect and a C compiler
notable: Staged curriculum where each stage covers one topic and has its own tests
Test runner can run all tests, one stage, or one test
Can validate the test suite itself by running it against bash or cat
Includes a list of language-specific guidance for writing a shell in Python, Rust, Haskell, Lua, OCaml, and others
Lists existing shells to examine, such as busybox ash, mksh, zsh, and fish
caveats: Work in progress; the README warns of infelicities and some flaky, timing-sensitive tests
Tests are described as less robust than ideal and written for pedagogy
Requires expect and a C compiler to run the tests
Stage 5 tests are not passed by dash, and the README notes minor compatibility differences with other shells
